title: The Baal Shem Tov
hook: Israel ben Eliezer, an eighteenth-century teacher in Podolia, taught that God is found in joy and simple devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday the taste of Talmud closed with Daf Yomi, the daily page. Your line was keep going together. Today, a new part of the path begins.

A village in what's now Ukraine, about three hundred years ago. Most of the Jews there are poor: farmers, innkeepers, peddlers, wagon drivers. Many can barely read the prayers, let alone a page of Talmud. The great scholars are far away, and sometimes what people hear is that real closeness to God belongs to the learned. Then a man starts walking from village to village with a very different message. His name was Israel ben Eliezer. People came to call him the Baal Shem Tov.
screen: `A VILLAGE, THREE HUNDRED YEARS AGO.` → `POOR, AND BARELY READING.` → `A DIFFERENT MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Baal Shem Tov means master of the good name; people often shorten it to the Besht. He lived in the 1700s, in the region called Podolia, and settled in the town of Medzhybizh. He wrote almost nothing himself. What we know comes through his students, and through a book of stories about him printed decades after his death, so it's hard to say where history stops and legend starts. His message, as his students taught it, fits in a sentence. God is everywhere, in every place and every moment, so every moment can be a way to God. Not only study and prayer, but eating, working, walking, talking with a neighbor. And the way in is joy. He's remembered for teaching that sadness shuts the heart, and that a person should serve God joyfully. His followers pointed to a line from the Psalms: "Serve the LORD with gladness." The movement that grew from his teaching is called Hasidism, and its followers Hasidim. Hasid is an old word, from the Hebrew chesed, loving-kindness; in the Psalms a hasid is a devoted, faithful one. Not everyone welcomed the movement at first; some leading rabbis, called Mitnagdim, opposed it strongly. Within a few generations the fiercest fighting had faded, and today both are part of Orthodox Jewish life. For the next weeks: Hasidic stories, short, surprising, and full of joy.
screen: `MASTER OF THE GOOD NAME.` · `GOD IN EVERY MOMENT.` · `SERVE WITH GLADNESS.` · `HASID: FROM CHESED, DEVOTION.` · then, large: `SERVE WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: A look back at this week: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, give me Yavneh, the white face, peace over precision, most from my students, a page a day. Now think of one ordinary task ahead of you, dishes, the commute, folding laundry, answering email, and picture doing it with a little joy on purpose: humming, noticing the warm water, being glad your hands work. Not pretending it's thrilling, just letting gladness in.
Hasid. A devoted one, from chesed, loving-kindness. The followers of the Baal Shem Tov, who taught that God is found in joy.
Your line: serve with joy. Every moment can be a way in, even the dishes. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hasidic communities today, such as Chabad, Satmar and Breslov, follow teachings that trace back to the Baal Shem Tov, and joyful song and dance, the niggun, are central to their prayer and gatherings.

That holiness lives only in synagogues, never in daily chores.

chat.meaning: As his students taught it, God is in every place and moment, so eating, working and walking can be ways to God. And the way in is joy.

Baal Shem Tov.meaning: Israel ben Eliezer, the founder of Hasidism; master of the good name

Besht.meaning: a short name for the Baal Shem Tov

Hasid.meaning: a devoted, faithful one; a follower of Hasidism

Mitnagdim.meaning: rabbis who opposed the early Hasidic movement

sources.work: Hasidic teachings attributed to the Baal Shem Tov

notes: Opens 'Hasidic stories' (days 294–313) and includes the week-end look-back for days 288–294.
Dates: the Baal Shem Tov c. 1698/1700–1760; settled in Medzhybizh (Międzybóż) c. 1740. Shivchei HaBesht printed 1814 (Kapust/Berdichev), Yiddish 1815.
The teaching on joy and against sadness is found in Tzava'at HaRivash and his students' works; attribution to the Besht himself is traditional.
Mitnagdim described neutrally; the Vilna Gaon's opposition is not named. Hasidic groups in howItsDone are examples only.
